newsitem.title: ITALY: Rash of global summits over - were they worth it?.
newsitem.headline: Rash of global summits over - were they worth it?.

text.p: By Nicholas Doughty, Diplomatic Correspondent

The fashion for global summits, tackling everything from women's rights to starvation and the environment, may finally be at an end as the world stumbles towards the close of a bloody and chaotic century.

The U.N.-sponsored World Food Summit in Rome, which ended on Sunday after five days, is expected to be the last top-level gathering of leaders for some time after a glut of meetings in the 1990s, from Rio de Janeiro to Beijing.
The declarations and action plans have been completed, at least on paper. The delegations and motorcades have gone.

But uncomfortable questions remain about whether such meetings help focus the world's attention on real problems, or whether they are simply costly junkets that further damage the battered credibility of the United Nations.
The end of the Cold War has seen hopes rise that the international community, no longer riven by the East-West divide, could tackle such issues on a global scale.
In 1992, it was the Earth Summit in Rio de Janeiro to address the environment. Two years later, leaders met to discuss population problems in Cairo.
Last year, it was poverty in Copenhagen and women's rights in Beijing. This year it was urban problems in Istanbul and food in Rome.

U.N. Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali described these meetings as "great forward-looking actions" and said the Rome summit, which pledged to reduce hunger in the world, marked "the culmination of a process of reflection".

Defenders of such meetings say they play a vital role in raising public consciousness and in getting governments to focus on problems that transcend narrow national interests -- even if results and real action are slow in coming.
"They do take the international community each time a step closer to common understanding," said Kay Killingsworth, secretary-general of the Rome summit.

No one disputes the scale of the problems. More than one billion people, around one-fifth of the world's population, live in poverty. Almost as many are starving. Our cities are exploding, our environment badly damaged.

But critics say global summits are often little more than talking-shops which underline differences between nations, resulting in vague commitments that represent the lowest common denominator and are then not implemented by governments.
Rome, held in the shadow of the refugee crisis in eastern Zaire, was no exception.

The final statement and "action plan" declaring that everyone has the right to access to food took more than two years to negotiate, while the debate was marked by sharp differences between rich and poor over how to achieve the aims.
A similar, ministerial-level conference in 1974 had pledged to eradicate hunger within a decade.

Aid agencies, women's groups and other non-governmental organisations regularly gather on the fringes of such meetings, calling for more radical action -- an end to arms exports or the cancellation of debt for poor nations, for example.

Along with many developing nations, they accuse rich countries of hogging most of the planet's wealth and of cutting aid to the poor. The world's wealthy say discipline and trade will help the developing world more than handouts.
Iraq, Cuba and Burundi, all countries subject to sanctions, complained bitterly that their people suffered the most.

Leaders from many of the world's rich nations did not even come to the Rome summit, reflecting a view in countries like the United States that such gatherings, each costing millions of dollars to stage, are wasteful.
Baroness Lynda Chalker, Britain's minister for overseas development, said the world should act, not talk at a time when the United Nations is on the verge of bankruptcy.

"I for one -- and there are many others -- think that implementing action plans for the benefit of our fellow human beings must be at the top of all our agendas, not more summits," she said in Rome. "We've had enough of them."
The real question, addressed by many speakers in Rome, is whether there is the will to go beyond fine-sounding declarations about hunger, poverty or environmental issues.

"While governments all over the world claim that they are aware of issues concerning hunger and poverty, political will that is so essential to tackle hunger seems to be lacking," said Indian Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda.
